meta: Robert Walsh at his writing table: Thomas Sully's portrait of 1814, passed down in the sitter's family until 1920.
about: Robert Walsh sits in a dark coat and white cravat with a hand raised to his head, his gaze turned aside. On the table in front of him lie an open book of handwritten pages, a quill and an inkwell. The portrait stayed with his descendants, first his grandson Dr. J. F. Walsh and then the grandson's son Henry. It was sold at the American Art Association in New York in 1920. The collector Thomas B. Clarke owned it later, and the Mellon Trust bought it in 1936 and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1947.

meta: A boy building a house of cards: Jean Siméon Chardin's picture of about 1737, owned by Catherine II of Russia.
about: A boy in a brown jacket, with a blue ribbon in his hair, sits at a green-covered table and carefully builds a house of cards. Loose cards and coins lie around him, and one card rests in an open drawer. The picture appeared in a catalogue of the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg in 1774, when Catherine II of Russia owned it. Andrew Mellon bought it in 1931. It came to the National Gallery of Art as a gift in 1937.

meta: Elizabeth Throckmorton in the habit of an English Augustinian canoness: Nicolas de Largillierre's portrait of 1729.
about: A woman in a white religious habit and a black veil holds a small book in her clasped hands. The inscription at the top names her as Elizabeth, daughter of Sir Robert Throckmorton, and the back records that Largillierre painted it in 1729. She was a canoness of the English Augustinian Dames. Her brother, Sir Robert, the 4th baronet, commissioned the portrait and hung it in the parlour of Weston Underwood in Buckinghamshire. By 1855 it had moved to the family manor house, Coughton Court in Warwickshire. It then passed down through the baronets.

meta: A funeral procession before a Gothic cathedral at sunset: Thomas Cole's The Return, signed and dated 1837.
about: A Gothic cathedral with tall spires rises beside large autumn trees in a meadow at sunset. A procession carries a figure on a litter past a horse and rider, and a stone monument stands at the left. Thomas Cole signed the monument and dated it. William P. Van Rensselaer of Albany commissioned the painting. By 1853 it belonged to William Wilson Corcoran in Washington, who gave it to the Corcoran Gallery of Art in 1869. The National Gallery of Art acquired it in 2014.
credit_line: Corcoran Collection (Gift of William Wilson Corcoran, 1869)

meta: Madame Uhring, painted for herself: Jean-Jacques Henner's portrait of 1890, later in the Chester Dale collection.
about: A woman in three-quarter profile faces left against a deep green background, lit so that her face glows. She wears a dark hat and a dark, high-collared garment. Madame Uhring commissioned the portrait herself. It was sold at the Galerie Georges Petit in Paris on 23 October 1925, and the collector Chester Dale of New York bought it. He bequeathed it to the National Gallery of Art in 1963.

meta: A memorial to Admiral Sir Clowdisley Shovell: Sebastiano and Marco Ricci's painting of 1725, commissioned for the Duke of Richmond.
about: A ruined classical setting holds a fountain with sea-creature sculptures, a seated marble lion and tall Corinthian columns, with figures in period and classical dress gathered in the foreground. Owen McSwiny commissioned the picture for Charles Lennox, the 2nd Duke of Richmond, and it was at Goodwood and in London by 1726. A signature on a stone says that Bastiano and Marco Ricci made it. The duke's heir sold it at Christie's in 1814. The Kress Foundation bought it in 1953 and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1961.

meta: Christ speaks with the Samaritan woman at a well: a predella panel by Perugino, painted between 1500 and 1505.
about: Two figures stand on either side of an octagonal stone well with a gilded pulley and bucket, and the woman wears a pink and blue dress and holds a terracotta water jar. The panel is one of four that once formed a predella, the row of small scenes at the foot of an altarpiece, together with a fifth showing the Resurrection that is now in the Metropolitan Museum. Each scene shows a moment when the divine nature of Jesus was revealed. The altarpiece above has not been identified. Martin Ryerson of Chicago bought the panels through Durand-Ruel in 1892.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

meta: Sea gods battling water satyrs in the marsh: the right half of Andrea Mantegna's Battle of the Sea Gods.
about: In marshy shallows three male sea gods fight each other and two water satyrs. The satyr on the left carries a club and a monster's head, and a sea nymph on his back looks away from the fight in fear. The satyr on the right, armed with a hatchet, struggles against the grip of a sea god behind him. Another sea god blows a horn to rouse the fighters. The third strikes left and right with two fish. Serpents and sea creatures lurk in the rushes behind.

meta: The Coronation of the Virgin with Saint Jerome and Saint John the Baptist: an engraving by the Master of the Die.
about: The Virgin and Christ sit at the centre, flanked by two angels who draw back curtains. God the Father appears in the upper register. Saint Jerome stands at the right with his lion, and Saint John the Baptist at the left. Two putti sit in the foreground. A dove of the Holy Spirit hovers above, and Christ places a crown on the kneeling Virgin.

meta: The Marriage of the Virgin and the Marriage Feast at Cana: a double drawing by Stradanus, with a sea battle on the back.
about: Two scenes sit side by side. On the left a priest stands on a podium with the Virgin and Joseph at either side, and guests surround them. On the right Christ sits at a large table at lower right beside wine casks, with the bride and groom in the background. The back of the sheet carries a different subject, a naval battle seen from a distance. Many tall-masted ships fill it, and some tilt at dangerous angles. A bridge crosses the middle.

meta: An ornate ewer with a grotesque handle: plate 12 of Enea Vico's series of vases, dated 1543 in Roman numerals.
about: An engraved ewer has a handle formed of an animal foot that joins a grotesque head with a twisted neck, and the head holds a dish in its mouth. On the body of the vase two figures pay homage to a herm. A tablet below carries an inscription saying the design was found in Rome from an antique original, with the date given in Roman numerals as 1543, and the initials A.E.V. This sheet is plate 12 of a series.

meta: An altar of the vine under a triple arch: Gabriel Huquier's design for the Gardens of Bacchus.
about: An altar hung with symbols of the grape stands in the centre of the design, with groups of figures on either side, set in a landscape. A triple hanging arch frames the scene. Below it sit a double shell with a dog and a goat. The framework around it is made of arabesques with herms, masks, garlands and bat-wing ornaments. Gabriel Huquier made the pen and gray wash drawing.

meta: A circus scene signed and dated 1889: the painting whose attribution to Suzanne Valadon is disputed.
about: Several authorities have rejected the attribution of this painting to Suzanne Valadon. Others support it. They argue that the picture is merely atypical because it is an early work, signed and dated 1889. Valadon did not begin to develop her mature style until 1891. She was the mother of the painter Maurice Utrillo and a prolific painter herself, although she never had formal artistic training. The Cleveland Museum of Art notes that she also modelled for Renoir and Toulouse-Lautrec.
credit_line: Bequest of Leonard C. Hanna Jr.

meta: Umbrella pines in the gardens of the Villa Borghese: Hendrik Voogd's Italian landscape, signed in Rome in 1807.
about: Tall umbrella pines rise above a sunlit grassy clearing in the gardens of the Villa Borghese in Rome. The Villa Giulia and Monte Mario lie in the background, and small figures gather at the lower left. Hendrik Voogd signed the painting with the words fecit Roma and the date 1807. The Rijksmuseum bought it at an anonymous sale in Vienna on 14 November 1976, where it cost 110,000 Swiss francs.

meta: The nymph Syrinx fleeing Pan: Jean François de Troy's mythological painting from about 1720.
about: In Ovid's Metamorphoses the nymph Syrinx flees the lecherous advances of the god Pan. Trapped at the edge of a river, she begs for a way out, and the gods turn her into reeds. Pan then gathers the reeds to make the pan pipes, which stay linked with him. The Cleveland Museum of Art says such subjects were a challenge, since they demanded skill with the body in complex poses and a knowledge of ancient texts. It adds that de Troy's rich colours and voluptuous figures suited the love stories his elite patrons favoured.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. William H. Marlatt Fund

meta: A nude faun asleep under a large tree: Carl Blechen's Sleeping Faun, sold in a forced sale in 1942 and restituted in 2009.
about: A nude figure reclines on a grassy bank beneath a large tree, with palm-like plants and a dusky sky over a distant coastline. The painting belonged to Julius Freund in Berlin, and after his death it passed to his estate. It was sold in a forced sale at the Galerie Fischer in Lucerne on 21 March 1942 and bought for the German Reich. In 1968 it went on loan to the Wallraf-Richartz-Museum. It was restituted in 2009.

meta: A vase of flowers beside a dead frog: Jacob Marrel's still life, signed and dated at Utrecht in 1634.
about: A richly ornamented metal vase overflows with tulips, roses and anemones on a pale stone ledge, and a dead frog and a cluster of white currants lie beside it. Marrel signed the picture on the table in the foreground, adding the place Utrecht and the date. It may be the flower piece sold in London on 7 January 1824 as a companion to another lot. The Hague painter Hendrik Willem Mesdag gave it to the museum in 1883.

meta: A dedication to Charles III of Spain: Giovanni Volpato's frontispiece for Paolantonio Paoli's book on the ruins of Paestum.
about: Genii place a bust of a man on a pedestal before a shining sun. The inscription dedicates the work to Charles III, the Catholic king, and says that Count Gazola offers and consecrates the book and himself to him. Below lie several attributes, among them a horn, a book, a palette and brushes. Above, a goddess sits on a cloud before a colonnaded building. Giovanni Volpato made the engraved page as the frontispiece for Paoli's Rovine della città di Pesto, published in 1784.

meta: A crowd at the races: a version of William Powell Frith's Derby Day, sold at Christie's as the original sketch.
about: A large gathering of people fills the open grass, with bunting on the tents, a carriage, a drummer and a grandstand packed with spectators under a cloudy sky. Ernest Gambart bought a version of Frith's Derby Day from the artist in 1857. At Christie's in London in 1861 it was offered as the original of the celebrated work shown at the Royal Academy. In 1881 another sale described it as the original completed sketch.
